question: When someone opens the sparks repo for the first time, what's the one thing you want them to understand sparks is for, and what problem in their work does it solve that nothing else does?
answer: Sparks is a way that, that helps users distill their intent, taste, skill, reasoning, expertise, and craft into projects so that agents creating verification skills inside can do work that is more, um, that, that, that is of higher quality and follows, um, and follows the desired path to success more, with more compliance. It also packages working styles, specification conventions, and orchestration logic and implementation to efficiently distribute tokens to the providers that any Grokbot operator uses for their work. Finally, it is Grokbot native and is intended to be installable into users' Grokbot accounts at the user level while also being installed into any repositories that follow the Sparks framework and working style while remaining invisible to the worker agents in the ways that should only be visible to Grokbot by constraining harness options and configuring the pi agents that run inside of the sanctioned herdr multiplexer accordingly.

question: You said sparks stays invisible to the worker agents and visible only to Grok Bot. What exactly should a worker agent see or feel from sparks while it works, and what must it never see?
answer: Well, the worker agents are going to have system prompts that the, uh, that the Sparks CLI injects at their, uh, spawning that, uh, that, um, cause them to invoke certain skills or behave in certain ways based on their persona. And so Sparks only wants worker agents to be launched with that persona. In terms of what they would feel, a reviewer agent, for example, would only have the review skills that Sparks packages visible, and an agent that is meant to write a spec from certain source like a call transcript or a sparks.json for a particular fix can only see that skill. And the implementer agents that take a spec or the tickets of a spec to implement them only see the Spark implementation skill, and so on and so forth with skills infinitely extensible and, um, specifiable in the dot TOML configuration of the agent type in the dot TOML file that is maintained with the setup Sparks skill.

question: When a spark and a worker's persona or skill disagree, say a sparks.json rule says one thing and the reviewer skill says another, which one wins, and who notices the conflict?
answer: The sparks.json wins and the agent reports the conflict to some source that is hitherto unspecified, but for now can be, for example, a file that the summoning Grokbot agents knows to look for. Uh, yeah, so what it can do is it can, um, write a gitignored, um, you know, uh, conflict report, and then the Grokbot agent that calls it can look at it and surface the contradictions to the user.

question: What does a good spark look like versus a bad one? If you had to judge whether a spark is worth keeping, what would you check?
answer: A good spark is one where, or rather the ideal spark is one where both the question and the answer were provided and curated by the user word for word. The question encodes assumptions about the work, and the spark lives in the directory closest to where it most often applies. However, the spark framework is made to be flexible in that ideally all of the sparks contribute to all work, and the way that this is done is that the spark CLI will soon be extended with its most important functionality, which is to programmatically determine and potentially with a vector store on top of the sparks as well, help agents identify the sparks that pertain most closely to their work.

question: Who is sparks for beyond you? Picture the first outside Grok Bot operator who installs it: what should they be able to do on day one, and what should they never have to learn?
answer: Sparks is for people who want to get the most out of Grokbot while being able to utilize their other subscriptions than the X subscription for the most demanding technical work, considering that there are many frontier models with different specialties, and that the Grok models packaged in a cursor subscription, for example, at maximum usage are not fast enough for everything, nor smart enough for everything, despite being well-balanced. And so Sparks enables any user to simply install it and no other skills into their cursor account and give their Grokbots access to it, and their Grokbots become hyper-capable users of herdr to orchestrate agents that comply extremely well and run in pi using whatever inference provider the user desires to complete all kinds of work, using not only the context provided in any given conversation, but indeed the context and user taste and user preference built up in every single interaction with any agents in that project, either through a Grokbot or directly through herdr. And it also allows anybody to bring their own harness and know exactly what kind of context is encoded in the sparks.json so that no matter what harness they use in a collaborative setting, um, operators, human operators, can get their agents to comply with the conventions and the desirable behaviors of a project on a project-by-project basis in a fashion that is easy to query, easy to update, and easy to trace thanks to the commit history, while also being easy to git ignore if people want to keep some context on their local machine, for example, and some context in remote. So the fact that Sparks offers extreme extensibility and allows users to make whatever they want out of context using these clearly defined rules makes it almost like a programming language in the sense that it empowers users through a single entry point to pilot very large, very accurate fleets of agents, whether they prefer voice, the terminal, the Grokbot application, or even mentions, considering that Sparks works very well with G D S R V N T slash mentions, which will likely be incorporated into Spark or supported first class in a very soon to come release.

question: You compared sparks to a programming language. What should sparks deliberately refuse to become, so it stays simple enough to trust?
answer: Well, Sparks does not try to replace things like agents.md for project context, nor does it aim to replace GitHub Issues for issue tracking, or Git for version control, or PRs for CI, or GitHub Actions for CD, for example. It is an overlay that can live over top of any of these while also not needing them because it simply tells agents how to behave inside of a project and works with the platform that I believe is the best in the world at liberating human time, and so it solves the only remaining deficit that Grokbot has, which is how to consistently and predictably integrate context into projects that accumulates over long periods of time without overwhelming the context of any one agent while allowing Grokbot, which is relatively locked down, to share context with all agents that it drives on behalf of the user.
